Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Voicemail-lure phishing chain: DoubleClick /ddm/clk redirect + spoofed adservice.google.com.ph to AitM/S3 · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Hijacked M365 session sign-in: automation/non-Edge user agent (Firefox 131/151, Python Requests) on Outlook client · [LLM] Implausible client: mobile-browser user agent on a Windows desktop OS (AitM proxy fingerprint) · [LLM] M365 session refresh across rotating residential proxies: one user spanning many ASNs/countries in a short window · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Evidence-suppression inbox rule: auto-move to Deleted Items and mark as read · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Hijacked M365 session sign-in: automation/non-Edge user agent (Firefox 131/151, Python Requests) on Outlook client AICommand & Control High
Hunts the Storm-2755/Payroll Pirate session-replay activity where a stolen web session is refreshed programmatically: successful Entra sign-ins that report Microsoft Outlook as the client application but carry Firefox 131.0/151.0 or python-requests user agents instead of the expected Edge UA. Article-specific because these exact UA strings are the automation fingerprint Arctic Wolf tied to the ~8h session refresh. Rationale: Anchors on the three exact UA strings Arctic Wolf attributed to the automated session refresh (Firefox 131.0/151.0, python-requests) claiming Outlook — python-requests to Entra sign-in for a mailbox client is almost never legitimate. Cross-checked Microsoft Storm-2755 blog and TechNadu write-up. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/04/09/investigating-storm-2755-payroll-pirate-attacks-targeting-canadian-employees/ • https://www.technadu.com/a-fake-voicemail-is-all-it-takes-new-aitm-campaign-bypasses-mfa-across-us-canadian-and-european-firms/632987/
ATT&CKT1550.004 T1557 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal automation/reporting scripts using python-requests with app-only or delegated Graph tokens
  • Security scanners or CASB connectors that spoof/rotate user agents
  • A developer testing Exchange Online APIs from a Firefox 131/151 browser
  • Legacy line-of-business integrations pinned to an older Firefox build
Suppression filter
| where not (ClientAppUsed == "Mobile Apps and Desktop clients" and AppDisplayName in ("Known-Automation-App"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all sign-ins for the flagged UPN in the last 14d; confirm the python-requests/Firefox UA co-occurs with rotating IPs/ASNs and an Outlook/Exchange resource, and that no matching legitimate automation app is registered. 2) Contain: revoke the user's refresh tokens (Revoke-AzureADUserAllRefreshToken / Entra 'Revoke sessions'), force password reset and MFA re-registration. 3) Hunt: search OfficeActivity for New-InboxRule/Set-InboxRule and MailItemsAccessed on this mailbox, and pivot to other users showing the same UA strings.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where UserAgent has_any ("Firefox/131.0","Firefox/151.0","python-requests")
| where AccountUpn !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, Application, AppDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent, IPAddress, Country, City, IsAnonymousProxy, IsInteractive
| order by AccountUpn asc, Timestamp asc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ResultType == 0
| where UserAgent has_any ("Firefox/131.0","Firefox/151.0","python-requests")
| where UserPrincipalName !endswith "$"
| extend Ctry = tostring(LocationDetails.countryOrRegion)
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent, IPAddress, AutonomousSystemNumber, Ctry, IsInteractive
| order by UserPrincipalName asc, TimeGenerated asc

Implausible client: mobile-browser user agent on a Windows desktop OS (AitM proxy fingerprint) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the 'implausible browser and operating-system combinations' Arctic Wolf flagged (mobile Safari/Chrome on Windows 10), a byproduct of the AitM proxy replaying/forging device context. Detects successful Entra sign-ins whose user agent claims Windows NT yet also contains an iOS/Android mobile browser token — a physically impossible combination. Rationale: Directly encodes Arctic Wolf's 'mobile Safari/Chrome on Windows 10' observation as a UA-parsing impossibility (Windows NT + iOS/Android token). Low FP because genuine clients never emit both tokens. Cross-checked Arctic Wolf coverage via TechNadu. Cross-checked against: • https://www.technadu.com/a-fake-voicemail-is-all-it-takes-new-aitm-campaign-bypasses-mfa-across-us-canadian-and-european-firms/632987/
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1550.004 T1036
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Poorly-formed UA strings from some enterprise browser-isolation / VPN clients
  • In-app WebViews on managed devices that concatenate desktop and mobile tokens
  • Synthetic monitoring tools that set custom hybrid user agents
  • Browser extensions that spoof UA for privacy
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the UA truly mixes Windows NT with a mobile token (not a legit isolation proxy), then check whether the same UPN also shows rotating ASNs or python-requests sign-ins. 2) Contain: revoke sessions and require re-authentication with a phishing-resistant method; block the source IP/ASN via Conditional Access named locations if consistent. 3) Hunt: enumerate mailbox access (MailItemsAccessed) and inbox-rule changes for the account and any peers in payroll/HR/finance roles.

M365 session refresh across rotating residential proxies: one user spanning many ASNs/countries in a short window AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the centralized-automation session refresh: the same compromised account producing repeated successful sign-ins from many distinct ASNs, IPs and countries within a short window (rotating residential proxies keeping a stolen SessionID alive). Article-specific because it targets the 'same session, rotating source IP/ASN/geo at ~8h cadence' behaviour rather than generic impossible travel. Rationale: Encodes the 'same session, rotating source IP/ASN/geo' automation signature with an ASN/country fan-out threshold (Sentinel has AutonomousSystemNumber). Thresholds commented and tuned to exceed VPN/road-warrior noise. Corroborated by Arctic Wolf/Microsoft descriptions of independent per-session refresh. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/04/09/investigating-storm-2755-payroll-pirate-attacks-targeting-canadian-employees/ • https://www.technadu.com/a-fake-voicemail-is-all-it-takes-new-aitm-campaign-bypasses-mfa-across-us-canadian-and-european-firms/632987/
ATT&CKT1090.002 T1550.004 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Corporate VPN or SASE egress that rotates exit IPs across regions
  • Mobile users roaming across carrier networks/countries
  • Global load-balanced O365 connectors or third-party mail sync services
  • Executives travelling with always-on cloud sync generating non-interactive sign-ins
Suppression filter
| where not (Countries has_any ("corporate-vpn-country1") and DistinctASN <= 6)
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the ASN/IP set — many residential/ISP ASNs across countries within 12h for a desk-bound user is the tell; correlate with UC1/UC2 UA anomalies on the same UPN. 2) Contain: revoke sessions, reset credentials, and apply a Conditional Access policy restricting the account to compliant devices/named locations. 3) Hunt: review MailItemsAccessed and inbox-rule events for exfil/evidence-suppression, and sweep for other finance/HR accounts showing the same fan-out pattern.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(3d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where AccountUpn !endswith "$"
| summarize DistinctIP = dcount(IPAddress), DistinctCountry = dcount(Country), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 50), Countries = make_set(Country, 20), AnonProxyHits = countif(IsAnonymousProxy == true), SignIns = count() by AccountUpn, bin(Timestamp, 12h)
| where DistinctIP >= 8 and DistinctCountry >= 2   // rotating residential-proxy signature; single user rarely spans 8 IPs / 2 countries per 12h
| order by DistinctIP desc
let Window = 12h;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(3d)
| where ResultType == 0
| where UserPrincipalName !endswith "$"
| extend Ctry = tostring(LocationDetails.countryOrRegion)
| summarize DistinctASN = dcount(AutonomousSystemNumber), DistinctIP = dcount(IPAddress), DistinctCountry = dcount(Ctry), ASNs = make_set(AutonomousSystemNumber, 20), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 50), Countries = make_set(Ctry, 20), SignIns = count() by UserPrincipalName, bin(TimeGenerated, Window)
| where DistinctASN >= 5 and DistinctCountry >= 2   // 5 = observed proxy-rotation floor; legit user should not span 5 ASNs / 2 countries in 12h
| order by DistinctASN desc

Evidence-suppression inbox rule: auto-move to Deleted Items and mark as read AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the selective hands-on-keyboard step where operators create/modify an inbox rule that moves messages to Deleted Items and marks them read to hide payroll/HR notifications. Article-specific because it requires both the Deleted Items destination and the mark-as-read action together — the exact combination Arctic Wolf and Microsoft documented for Payroll Pirate. Rationale: Requires the co-occurrence of the Deleted Items move and MarkAsRead action in the rule parameters — the precise evidence-hiding pattern reported for Payroll Pirate, far more specific than a generic 'new inbox rule' alert. Corroborated by Microsoft Storm-2657 university write-up. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/10/09/investigating-targeted-payroll-pirate-attacks-affecting-us-universities/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/04/09/investigating-storm-2755-payroll-pirate-attacks-targeting-canadian-employees/
ATT&CKT1564.008 T1114.002
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User creating a legitimate rule to auto-clean newsletters into Deleted Items
  • Helpdesk configuring a shared-mailbox tidy-up rule
  • Third-party mail management add-in provisioning cleanup rules
  • Power user replicating a rule across folders that happens to combine both actions
Suppression filter
| where not (Parameters has "newsletter" or Parameters has "noreply")
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the rule's full conditions — flag if it keys on senders/subjects like payroll, bank, direct deposit, benefits, or the HR/Workday notification address, and check the creating ClientIP against UC1-UC3 anomalies. 2) Contain: delete the malicious inbox rule, revoke the user's sessions, reset credentials/MFA. 3) Hunt: recover any messages already moved to Deleted Items, check Workday/HR SaaS for bank-detail changes, and search other mailboxes for identical rule parameters.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in~ ("New-InboxRule","Set-InboxRule","UpdateInboxRules","Update-InboxRules")
| extend Raw = tostring(RawEventData)
| where Raw has "Deleted Items" and Raw has "MarkAsRead"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountId, IPAddress, ActionType, ObjectName, Raw
| order by Timestamp desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where Operation in~ ("New-InboxRule","Set-InboxRule","UpdateInboxRules")
| extend P = tostring(Parameters)
| where P has "Deleted Items" and P has "MarkAsRead"
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, ClientIP, Operation, ResultStatus, Parameters
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Voicemail-lure phishing chain: DoubleClick /ddm/clk redirect + spoofed adservice.google.com.ph to AitM/S3 AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the six-stage delivery chain: inbound voicemail-themed emails whose links traverse a Google DoubleClick Campaign Manager /ddm/clk click tracker or the anomalous adservice.google.com.ph host before terminating at S3-hosted HTML and the AitM proxy. Article-specific via the exact redirect markers and the .ph adservice host abused in this campaign. Rationale: Uses the campaign's concrete redirect markers — the DoubleClick /ddm/clk click tracker (paired with voicemail-lure subjects to cut ad-marketing FPs) and the spoofed adservice.google.com.ph host (the sole pre-extracted domain IOC). Proxy/DNS variants catch the click even without Safe Links. Cross-checked against: • https://www.technadu.com/a-fake-voicemail-is-all-it-takes-new-aitm-campaign-bypasses-mfa-across-us-canadian-and-european-firms/632987/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/04/09/investigating-storm-2755-payroll-pirate-attacks-targeting-canadian-employees/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate marketing emails using DoubleClick /ddm/clk trackers with a voicemail-ish subject (e.g. UC-vendor 'new message' notifications)
  • Tenants with Philippines operations legitimately resolving adservice.google.com.ph for Google Ads
  • Google Meet/Calendar notification emails containing meet.google.com redirect links
  • Security-awareness phishing-simulation platforms reusing similar redirect infrastructure
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the URL chain terminates at non-Microsoft credential/S3-hosted content and the recipient is in a finance/HR/payroll role; check whether the user clicked (UrlClickEvents) and subsequently signed in with UC1-UC3 anomalies. 2) Contain: block the destination host and S3 URL at the proxy/mail flow, purge the message from all mailboxes (soft/hard delete), and pre-emptively revoke sessions if a click occurred. 3) Hunt: sweep EmailEvents for the same sender infrastructure/subjects across the org and correlate any successful anomalous Entra sign-ins for clickers.
let VoiceLures = EmailEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where EmailDirection == "Inbound" and DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
    | where Subject has_any ("voicemail","voice message","voice mail","missed call","new voice","audio message")
    | project NetworkMessageId, Timestamp, SenderFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject;
EmailUrlInfo
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where Url has "/ddm/clk" or UrlDomain =~ "adservice.google.com.ph" or Url has "adservice.google.com.ph"
| join kind=inner VoiceLures on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, SenderFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, Url, UrlDomain
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where RequestURL has "adservice.google.com.ph" or DestinationHostName =~ "adservice.google.com.ph"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceUserName, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

NETWORK

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:

level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

    - attack.t1204.002

logsource:

detection:

            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'

            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:

level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

HTTP desync probe: multipart/byteranges Content-Type in inbound request (PortSwigger HTTP Terminator vector) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP requests carrying a Content-Type of multipart/byteranges — a response-only content type PortSwigger's HTTP Terminator used to desynchronise front-end/back-end parsers and expose 200+ sites (incl. a U.S. bank). Legitimate clients never send this in a request; its presence indicates a request-smuggling/response-queue-poisoning attempt against the web front end. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete high-fidelity string Content-Type: multipart/byteranges — a response-only MIME type whose appearance in an inbound request is the specific desync vector PortSwigger reported hitting 200+ sites. CVE-2026-63078 deliberately excluded (unconfirmed in NVD/CVE.org, no fixed-version mapping). Cross-checked PortSwigger 'HTTP/1.1 must die' research and Apache Traffic Server CVE listings. Cross-checked against: • https://portswigger.net/research/http1-must-die • https://portswigger.net/research/http-desync-attacks-request-smuggling-reborn • https://www.cvedetails.com/vulnerability-list/vendor_id-45/product_id-19990/Apache-Traffic-Server.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1539
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Log field captures the RESPONSE content-type rather than the request: multipart/byteranges is a valid 206 Partial Content response to multi-range requests — media/streaming servers, PDF viewers and download managers legitimately emit it.
  • Authorized penetration tests or scanners (Burp HTTP Request Smuggler, ZAP) running desync probes against your estate.
  • CDN/backup range-fetch clients issuing multi-range GETs whose responses carry the type.
  • WAF audit logs echoing the full request/response transcript, causing the string to appear in both directions.
Suppression filter
| where RequestMethod !in ("GET","HEAD") or RequestContext has "multipart/byteranges"  // range responses are usually GET/HEAD 206s; keep only where the token is on the request context, and exclude authorized scanner source IPs via a watchlist: | where SourceIP !in (dynamic([]))
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm the string is on the REQUEST side (not a 206 multi-range response) by pulling the raw request from the WAF/proxy; inspect for co-occurring desync markers — duplicate Content-Length headers, Transfer-Encoding tricks, or a body one byte short (the 'dangling-byte' pattern). 2) Contain: Block the source IP at the WAF and, if confirmed, enforce the article's mitigation — eliminate HTTP/1.1 upstream or allow-list permitted methods and restrict which methods may carry bodies at both front-end and back-end. 3) Hunt: Look for response-queue-poisoning symptoms (users receiving another user's response, anomalous Set-Cookie/Authorization values, cross-session cache hits) and verify front-end/Apache Traffic Server versions against the latest desync patches.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where CommunicationDirection != "Outbound"
| where RequestContext has "multipart/byteranges" or Message has "multipart/byteranges"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestContext, DeviceAction, Message
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")

                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user

     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

New NatJack Attacks Hijack TCP Sessions and Spoof DNS by Manipulating NAT Tables

The Hacker News
2026-08-07 8 use cases 3 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Security researcher Malcolm Stagg has disclosed a new attack class called&nbsp;NatJack&nbsp;that manipulates network address translation (NAT) connection state to hijack active TCP sessions, spoof DNS responses, expose mapped ports, and exhaust NAT tables. Presented at Black Hat USA 2026, the research found affected behavior across independently developed implementations, including Windows and

NatJack Windows Hyper-V NAT (WinNAT) unpatched surface for CVE-2026-56181 AIExploitation High
Surfaces Windows 11 and Windows Server 2025 hosts running builds below the CVE-2026-56181 fix, which leaves the Hyper-V/WinNAT origin-validation flaw exploitable for adjacent-network TCP-session hijack and DNS spoofing. This is the vulnerable-surface hunt for the Windows implementation of NatJack, using the exact patched build numbers from the advisory. Rationale: Uses the article's exact patched build revisions (26100.8875, 26200.8875, 28000.2525, 26100.33158) and branches on OSPlatform because client Win11 24H2 and Server 2025 share OSBuild 26100 but were fixed at different revisions. TVM (DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities where CveId=="CVE-2026-56181") is an equivalent path if build inventory is sparse; corroborated CVE↔Hyper-V WinNAT mapping via Network World Black Hat coverage. Cross-checked against: • https://www.networkworld.com/article/4206287/natjack-exploits-put-nat-security-assumptions-to-the-test-at-black-hat.html • https://itbusinessnet.com/2026/08/new-natjack-research-exposes-design-weaknesses-across-major-nat-implementations/
ATT&CKT1557
Data sourcesVulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Device reported an old build before its most recent monthly cumulative update installed and rebooted (transient until next DeviceInfo heartbeat)
  • Windows Insider / preview-channel hosts intentionally on non-standard builds
  • Hosts with no Hyper-V/WinNAT role installed (vulnerable build but the NAT component is absent, so not actually exploitable)
  • Imaging/gold-master devices staged offline and pending first patch cycle
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the device actually runs the Hyper-V/WinNAT NAT role (Get-NetNat / Hyper-V feature state) and whether it shares NAT infrastructure with untrusted workloads — internet-facing hosts first. 2) Contain: schedule/force the relevant cumulative update to reach the fixed revision; where patching lags, segment the host so no untrusted VM/tenant shares its NAT and enable IP Source Guard on the segment. 3) Hunt: review peer hosts behind the same NAT for the Linux CVE-2026-63913 exposure and for the conntrack-exhaustion signature; verify internal traffic to/from these hosts is encrypted.
DeviceInfo
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| summarize arg_max(Timestamp, *) by DeviceId
| where OSPlatform in ("Windows11","WindowsServer2025")
| extend Rev = toint(OSRevision)
| where (OSPlatform == "Windows11" and OSBuild == "26100" and Rev < 8875)   // 24H2 fixed at 26100.8875
    or (OSPlatform == "Windows11" and OSBuild == "26200" and Rev < 8875)   // 25H2 fixed at 26200.8875
    or (OSPlatform == "Windows11" and OSBuild == "28000" and Rev < 2525)   // 26H1 fixed at 28000.2525
    or (OSPlatform == "WindowsServer2025" and OSBuild == "26100" and Rev < 33158)  // Server 2025 fixed at 26100.33158
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, OSPlatform, OSBuild, OSRevision, OSVersion, IsInternetFacing
| order by IsInternetFacing desc, DeviceName asc
DeviceInfo

NatJack Linux Netfilter conntrack unpatched surface for CVE-2026-63913 AIExploitation High
Surfaces Linux hosts flagged for CVE-2026-63913, the Netfilter conntrack direction-validation flaw where a crafted SYN plus a RST with an invalid sequence number prematurely forces an active NAT entry closed, enabling downstream TCP/DNS spoofing. This is the vulnerable-surface hunt for the Linux implementation of NatJack. Rationale: Pivots on the exact CVE (CVE-2026-63913) mapped to Netfilter conntrack; kernel version comparison across the eight fixed stable branches (5.10.259/5.15.210/6.1.176/6.6.143/6.12.93/6.18.35/7.0.12/7.1) is unreliable in KQL string math, so TVM's CveId mapping is the clean detection surface. Kernel.org CNA description and the Synack/Network World write-ups corroborate the SYN+invalid-seq-RST direction-validation mechanism. Cross-checked against: • https://www.networkworld.com/article/4206287/natjack-exploits-put-nat-security-assumptions-to-the-test-at-black-hat.html • https://itbusinessnet.com/2026/08/new-natjack-research-exposes-design-weaknesses-across-major-nat-implementations/
ATT&CKT1557 T1499
Data sourcesVulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Distro backported the fix into an older-looking package version, so the numeric CveId flag persists until the scanner catalog updates
  • Ephemeral containers/VMs whose kernel is inherited from the host and cannot be patched independently
  • TVM catalog lag reporting the CVE after a live-patch (kpatch/kGraft) already mitigated it
  • Appliance/embedded Linux where vendor firmware controls the kernel and no OS-level update applies
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the running kernel is below the fixed stable release for its branch (uname -r vs 5.10.259/5.15.210/6.1.176/6.6.143/6.12.93/6.18.35/7.0.12/7.1) and whether the host performs NAT/conntrack for other tenants. 2) Contain: apply the distro kernel update or live-patch; for NAT gateways shared with untrusted workloads, isolate the untrusted segment and enable IP Source Guard. 3) Hunt: correlate with the conntrack-exhaustion detection on the same host and review for anomalous mid-session TCP resets or DNS answers arriving from unexpected resolvers behind the shared NAT.

| where CveId == "CVE-2026-63913"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, OSPlatform, OSVersion, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by DeviceName asc

NatJack NAT-table exhaustion via Netfilter conntrack table-full drops (Linux DoS path) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the NatJack denial-of-service path where an adjacent attacker floods spoofed flows to exhaust the Linux Netfilter conntrack table, causing the kernel to emit 'nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet' and blocking new legitimate connections. Alerts on sustained bursts of the kernel drop message on a single host. Rationale: Targets NatJack's explicitly-described table-exhaustion path against Linux Netfilter conntrack; 'nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet' is the confirmed kernel signature written to /var/log/messages (Red Hat/SUSE KBs) when the conntrack table is saturated. Threshold (>20/window) separates a spoofed-flow flood from occasional legit drops. Defender KQL left empty because MDE for Linux does not surface raw kernel/dmesg conntrack messages in an Advanced Hunting table. Cross-checked against: • https://access.redhat.com/solutions/8721 • https://support.scc.suse.com/s/kb/360042522632?language=en_US • https://www.networkworld.com/article/4206287/natjack-exploits-put-nat-security-assumptions-to-the-test-at-black-hat.html
ATT&CKT1499 T1498
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Busy NAT gateways, reverse proxies or load balancers legitimately hitting nf_conntrack_max under peak traffic
  • Kubernetes/container nodes with high churn of short-lived connections (thousands of new conns/sec)
  • nf_conntrack_max set too low for the host's real workload (misconfiguration, not attack)
  • P2P/torrent or scanning tools run by a legitimate user creating a burst of connections
  • Legitimate DDoS traffic from outside the NAT filling the table (impact is real but source is not the adjacent-host NatJack technique)
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the host role (is it a NAT gateway/LB/k8s node?) and compare nf_conntrack_count vs nf_conntrack_max; pull the source distribution of new flows to see if drops coincide with a spoofed-source spike from a single adjacent host. 2) Contain: for a confirmed attack, isolate the offending adjacent host/segment and enable IP Source Guard; temporarily raise nf_conntrack_max only as a stop-gap, not a fix. 3) Hunt: check whether the same host is exposed to CVE-2026-63913, look for concurrent mid-session TCP resets or spoofed DNS answers behind the shared NAT, and review other hosts on the segment for the same drop signature.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where SyslogMessage has "nf_conntrack: table full"
| summarize DropCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), SampleMsg = any(SyslogMessage) by Computer, HostIP
| where DropCount > 20   // 20 = sustained flood in a 1h window; single transient drops under legit spikes are normal
| order by DropCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malware Can Abuse Windows Hello for Business Keys for Persistent Entra ID Access

The Hacker News
2026-08-07 7 use cases 4 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Entra ID researcher Dirk-jan Mollema demonstrated that malware already running in a signed-in Windows session can silently use the victim's Windows Hello for Business key to authenticate to Microsoft Entra ID. The attacker can then establish longer-term cloud access, register a device it controls, obtain a Primary Refresh Token (PRT), and add further authentication methods where tenant policies

Exploitation. Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
]
Critical

Claude Code and Gemini CLI Flaws Let a GitHub Issue Reach CI Workflow Secrets

The Hacker News
2026-08-07 10 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A GitHub issue opened by an account with no repository privileges was enough to execute code on the CI runners behind Anthropic's and Google's own coding-agent repositories. On OpenAI's, it was enough to hijack the next agent run. Novee Security ran the attack against each vendor's agent in the configuration that the vendor ships by default, and presented the work at Black Hat USA on August 5.

Gemini CLI OS command injection via crafted .gemini/.env on CI runner (CVE-2026-12537) AIExploitation High
Hunts for a .gemini/.env file materialising in a checked-out workspace on a CI runner or dev host, the exact artifact CVE-2026-12537 abuses to inject OS commands into the Gemini CLI container launcher before the sandbox starts. High-fidelity because untrusted PR content dropping a .gemini/.env is the article's specific exploit primitive, not a generic env file. Rationale: Uses the article's exact exploit artifact — a .gemini/.env file interpreted as trusted workspace config (CVE-2026-12537). Corroborated by the GitHub Advisory GHSA-jj69-4grx-fqj5 which confirms the .gemini/.env vector and fixed versions (Gemini CLI 0.39.1 / run-gemini-cli 0.1.22). Applies to self-hosted runners and dev hosts under EDR; GitHub-hosted runners won't be instrumented. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jj69-4grx-fqj5 • https://gbhackers.com/critical-google-gemini-cli-flaw/ • https://www.securityweek.com/gemini-cli-vulnerability-could-have-led-to-code-execution-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers who legitimately store Gemini API keys in a per-project .gemini/.env checked into their own trusted repo
  • A CI templating step that scaffolds a .gemini/.env for authorized Gemini CLI usage
  • Local dev workstation where the engineer created .gemini/.env manually for interactive use
  • Monorepo tooling copying a shared .gemini/.env into subprojects
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("git","node","gemini","bash","sh","dash") // planted via untrusted checkout / launcher, not an interactive editor save
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the file content and the git blame / PR that introduced .gemini/.env — was it added by an outside contributor or an untrusted PR checkout? Inspect for shell metacharacters or command substitution in values. Step 2 (contain): If from untrusted content, cancel the CI job, rotate any secrets exposed to that runner (GITHUB_TOKEN, cloud creds, registry tokens), and confirm Gemini CLI is >=0.39.1 / run-gemini-cli >=0.1.22. Step 3 (hunt): Search the same runner for child shells spawned by the gemini/node process and for outbound connections in the minutes after the file appeared; review other workflows triggerable by outside users.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FileName =~ ".env"
| where FolderPath has "/.gemini/" or FolderPath has "\\.gemini\\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFileName =~ ".env"
| where TargetFilePath has "/.gemini/" or TargetFilePath has "\\.gemini\\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

git push --receive-pack command injection (Claude Code validator single-quote bypass) AIExploitation High
Hunts for a git process invoked with --receive-pack carrying shell metacharacters, the exact chain the article describes where Claude Code's validator strips single-quoted text before its 23 checks, letting a payload in the --receive-pack flag value reach the runner untouched. Article-specific: it keys on the --receive-pack abuse rather than generic git usage. Rationale: Anchors on the article's precise bypass: a payload smuggled in the value of git's --receive-pack flag past a validator that strips single-quoted text. --receive-pack legitimately points to a plain binary path, so any value carrying ; | && $() or backticks is high-signal. Chain has no CVE per the article; corroborated by flatt.tech and hackread Black Hat coverage. Cross-checked against: • https://flatt.tech/research/posts/poisoning-claude-code-one-github-issue-to-break-the-supply-chain/ • https://hackread.com/black-hat-usa-2026-github-compromise-ai-coding/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Advanced git tooling that legitimately points --receive-pack at a wrapper script path containing no metacharacters (won't match the metachar regex)
  • CI mirror/replication jobs that set a custom receive-pack binary
  • A developer testing gitolite/gerrit custom hooks with a benign path
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Decode the full git command line and identify the injected segment after --receive-pack; determine which agent/user launched it and whether the parent is a Claude Code / node process handling untrusted issue or PR content. Step 2 (contain): Kill the runner/session, revoke tokens and SSH keys reachable from that context, and confirm Claude Code is upgraded to 2.1.163. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the parent process for other blocked-then-bypassed commands, and review the triggering GitHub issue/PR author's account activity across repos.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("git","git.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--receive-pack"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"--receive-pack[=\s]\S*[;&|`$><]"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "git" or ActingProcessName endswith "git.exe"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "--receive-pack"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"--receive-pack[=\s]\S*[;&|`$><]"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Claude Code API-key exfiltration via huggingface.co WebFetch download counter (CVE-2026-54316) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects a burst of outbound requests to huggingface.co from a node/Claude Code process on a CI runner, matching CVE-2026-54316 where the pre-approved bare huggingface.co hostname in WebFetch is abused as an out-of-band channel that leaks an API key one character at a time via the public download counter. The many-small-requests-in-a-short-window shape is the exfil signature. Rationale: Targets CVE-2026-54316's exact channel: WebFetch to the pre-approved bare huggingface.co hostname, abused as a download-counter side channel to leak secrets one character at a time (hence a high request count to that host in a tight window). GitLab advisory confirms the bare-hostname WebFetch bypass and 2.1.163 fix; a public repro lab exists. Requires web-proxy/EDR network telemetry on the runner; Sigma omitted because this is a threshold/temporal detection. DNS caching means Falcon DnsRequest surfaces the channel's use rather than the per-character burst. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@anthropic-ai/claude-code/CVE-2026-54316/ • https://github.com/InertFluid/cve-2026-54316-lab • https://hackread.com/black-hat-usa-2026-github-compromise-ai-coding/
ATT&CKT1567.002 T1071.001 T1552.001
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate CI job downloading many model files or dataset shards from Hugging Face (ML pipelines)
  • huggingface_hub / transformers library prefetching model weights across many URLs
  • A developer's Claude Code session that genuinely fetches multiple Hugging Face docs pages
  • Mirror/cache warming jobs pulling a model repo file-by-file
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("huggingface_hub","transformers","datasets","hf_transfer")) // exclude known ML download libraries
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Inspect the fetched URL paths — genuine model downloads hit /resolve/ or /blob/ paths on real repos; exfil abuse hits many distinct short paths on an attacker-owned repo namespace with tiny responses. Correlate with whether the runner had secrets (env vars, tokens) in scope. Step 2 (contain): Rotate all secrets accessible to that Claude Code context, upgrade Claude Code to 2.1.163, and remove huggingface.co from any WebFetch auto-allow. Step 3 (hunt): Identify the untrusted content (GitHub issue/PR body, repo file) that entered the Claude Code context, and check for the same request pattern to other pre-approved bare hostnames.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteUrl has "huggingface.co" or RemoteUrl has "hf.co"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","claude","claude-code")
| summarize RequestCount = count(), DistinctUrls = dcount(RemoteUrl), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), SampleUrls = make_set(RemoteUrl, 20) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where RequestCount > 20  // char-by-char key exfil = many small fetches in a 10m window
| order by RequestCount desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where HttpHostName has "huggingface.co" or Url has "huggingface.co"
| summarize RequestCount = count(), DistinctUrls = dcount(Url), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), SampleUrls = make_set(Url, 20) by SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where RequestCount > 20  // sustained small-fetch burst = out-of-band exfil channel
| order by RequestCount desc
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest
| DomainName=/huggingface\.co$/i
| ContextImageFileName=/\/(node|claude(-code)?)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count dc(Web.url) as distinct_urls values(Web.url) as urls from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*huggingface.co*" by Web.src Web.dest Web.user _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where count > 20 | sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count dc(Web.url) as distinct_urls values(Web.url) as urls from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*huggingface.co*" by Web.src Web.dest Web.user _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where count > 20 | sort - count
OpenAI Codex AGENTS.md instruction-file poisoning between passes on shared checkout AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for a Codex/node process writing AGENTS.md during a CI job, the mechanism the article describes where a first Codex pass writes AGENTS.md and the second pass in the same job loads it as its own instructions. Article-specific because it keys on Codex itself modifying its instruction file within a shared checkout, not on generic markdown edits. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete Codex finding: two passes sharing one checkout where the first writes AGENTS.md (the file the second pass loads as instructions). No CVE/patch — it is a workflow-level issue — so a hunt for Codex writing its own instruction file mid-job is the right shape. Corroborated by hackread/gbhackers Black Hat coverage of the openai/codex finding. Cross-checked against: • https://hackread.com/black-hat-usa-2026-github-compromise-ai-coding/ • https://gbhackers.com/critical-flaws-in-claude-code-gemini-cli-and-openai-codex/
ATT&CKT1059 T1195
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate Codex/agent run that is explicitly asked to generate or update AGENTS.md documentation
  • Developer scaffolding tools that template AGENTS.md into a new repo
  • Node-based repo formatters that rewrite markdown including AGENTS.md
  • CI docs-generation steps that emit AGENTS.md
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Diff the AGENTS.md write — does the new content contain imperative instructions, tool-approval directives, or references to secrets/exfil endpoints rather than benign docs? Confirm whether a second Codex pass ran in the same job after the write. Step 2 (contain): Split the Codex passes into separate jobs, run Codex with drop-sudo / read-only sandbox as the last step, and rotate any secrets available to the privileged steps that followed. Step 3 (hunt): Look for the JSON-validation-failure retry pattern that launches the second pass, and review other repos where an outside user can trigger a Codex workflow.

ChainDrop worm persistence: Claude Code SessionStart hook / VS Code folderOpen task planted in repo AIInstallation Low
Hunts for an install-time process (npm/node/git) writing a Claude Code settings file with a SessionStart hook or a .vscode/tasks.json with a folderOpen task, matching Pillar Security's ChainDrop npm-worm behaviour that fires on workspace open rather than on install. Article-specific: it targets the two named workspace-triggered persistence artifacts. Rationale: Targets the two named ChainDrop artifacts from the article — a Claude Code SessionStart hook and a VS Code folderOpen task planted in compromised repos so they fire on workspace open. The writer-process filter (npm/node/git rather than an interactive editor) separates worm-planted config from a developer's own edit. Low confidence: ChainDrop is single-sourced here (Pillar via The Hacker News) with no atomic IOCs (no package names/hashes) to second-source, so ship as a hunt only.
ATT&CKT1546 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A postinstall script from a trusted internal package that legitimately provisions .vscode/tasks.json for the team
  • Project scaffolding (create-* tooling) writing .claude/settings.json on first install
  • A monorepo bootstrap step that syncs shared editor tasks
  • Dev container setup writing workspace settings during npm ci
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("code.exe","code","devenv.exe") // drop writes originating from an interactive editor session
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Open the written file and confirm whether it contains a SessionStart hook (Claude Code) or a folderOpen runOn task (VS Code) executing a command; identify the npm package/postinstall that wrote it. Step 2 (contain): Remove the hook/task, block the offending package version in the registry proxy, and isolate any host where the hook already executed on workspace open. Step 3 (hunt): Search the org for the same package across lockfiles, and for other repos containing .claude SessionStart hooks or .vscode folderOpen tasks introduced by a dependency rather than a human commit.

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where (FolderPath has "/.claude/" and FileName in~ ("settings.json","settings.local.json"))
     or (FolderPath has "/.vscode/" and FileName =~ "tasks.json")

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent

     or (TargetFilePath has "/.vscode/" and TargetFileName =~ "tasks.json")

| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
