File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("d30b4ea6f68456672f5abb35e9dcf7d54226372b66e9d60a7ee26b7a52568e74", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "b27b82afa5f15512f3856e549fb83d873fd0049759a4b62ce64c8d7d4dc2c678") or SHA1 in~ ("d30b4ea6f68456672f5abb35e9dcf7d54226372b66e9d60a7ee26b7a52568e74", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "b27b82afa5f15512f3856e549fb83d873fd0049759a4b62ce64c8d7d4dc2c678") or MD5 in~ ("d30b4ea6f68456672f5abb35e9dcf7d54226372b66e9d60a7ee26b7a52568e74", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "b27b82afa5f15512f3856e549fb83d873fd0049759a4b62ce64c8d7d4dc2c678")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("d30b4ea6f68456672f5abb35e9dcf7d54226372b66e9d60a7ee26b7a52568e74", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "b27b82afa5f15512f3856e549fb83d873fd0049759a4b62ce64c8d7d4dc2c678") or SHA1 in~ ("d30b4ea6f68456672f5abb35e9dcf7d54226372b66e9d60a7ee26b7a52568e74", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "b27b82afa5f15512f3856e549fb83d873fd0049759a4b62ce64c8d7d4dc2c678") or MD5 in~ ("d30b4ea6f68456672f5abb35e9dcf7d54226372b66e9d60a7ee26b7a52568e74", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "b27b82afa5f15512f3856e549fb83d873fd0049759a4b62ce64c8d7d4dc2c678")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["d30b4ea6f68456672f5abb35e9dcf7d54226372b66e9d60a7ee26b7a52568e74", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "b27b82afa5f15512f3856e549fb83d873fd0049759a4b62ce64c8d7d4dc2c678"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] UNC6671 passkey/Okta AiTM phishing domain resolution from endpoints · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] M365/Okta sign-in from UNC6671 AiTM proxy & residential-proxy infrastructure · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Automated bulk cloud data exfiltration via python-requests / PowerShell user-agents · [LLM] Rapid multi-cloud SSO application enumeration after single sign-in · [LLM] Post-compromise deletion of security & password-reset emails from mailbox · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
UNC6671 passkey/Okta AiTM phishing domain resolution from endpoints AIDelivery High
Hunts endpoints resolving or connecting to the specific passkey/Okta-themed AiTM credential-harvesting domains UNC6671 uses for vishing-driven MFA-enrollment lures. Victim-specific subdomains are appended to these shared root domains, so endswith/subdomain matching is used. Rationale: Uses the 20 exact passkey/Okta AiTM root domains from the article's IOC list, confirmed in GTIG's IOC table; endswith/subdomain matching accounts for the victim-specific subdomains GTIG documents (e.g. company.createpasskey.com). Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/unc6671-targets-financial-services-and-enterprise-cloud-environments • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/blackfile-vishing-extortion-operation/ • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/redact-extortion-group-blackfile/
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1557 T1539
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security-awareness/phishing-simulation tooling that pre-visits reported malicious domains
  • SOC analyst or IR responder manually browsing a reported domain during triage from a corporate host
  • Threat-intel sandbox/detonation VM sharing endpoint telemetry
  • Web proxy prefetch/link-preview services resolving the domain without user intent
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe") or DeviceName has_any ("phishsim","sandbox","detonation"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the user/host that resolved the domain and whether an actual HTTP session followed; pull the Okta/Entra sign-in history for that user in the same window. 2) Contain: revoke all active sessions and refresh tokens for the user, force password reset, and re-register MFA/passkey from a trusted device; block the domain and its resolved IPs at the proxy/DNS. 3) Hunt: pivot on the resolved IP across all endpoints for other resolvers, check for successful M365/Okta sign-ins from UNC6671 infra IPs, and review the user's inbox for deleted security/password-reset mail.

M365/Okta sign-in from UNC6671 AiTM proxy & residential-proxy infrastructure AIExploitation Medium
Alerts on interactive or non-interactive cloud sign-ins sourced from the specific UNC6671 AiTM reverse-proxy, phishing-backend, exfil, and residential-proxy IPs. These IPs front the AiTM session-cookie replay and the automated cloud access that follows credential theft. Rationale: All 11 IPs are from the article's IOC list and are categorised in GTIG's write-up (AS51852 Private Layer AiTM proxies, MEVSPACE/DDOS-GUARD phishing backends, exfil IPs, and AT&T/Comcast residential proxies used to authenticate from expected geos). A /32 sign-in match is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/unc6671-targets-financial-services-and-enterprise-cloud-environments • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hedge-fund-cyberattacks-tied-to-blackfile-linked-unc6671-extortion-group/
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1550.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate employee genuinely behind an AT&T/Comcast/Optimum residential IP that briefly overlaps a listed /32 (the four residential-proxy IPs carry higher FP risk than the dedicated hosting IPs)
  • Security vendor scanning/validation from an overlapping IP
  • Threat-intel enrichment/IOC-validation service replaying the IP
  • VPN egress reassignment on a consumer ISP reusing a listed address
Suppression filter
| where not (IPAddress in ("107.128.45.122","76.103.148.180","38.42.59.171","47.218.103.146") and ConditionalAccessStatus == "success" and IsInteractive == true and ErrorCode == 0 and ClientAppUsed == "Browser")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the account, app, and whether the sign-in succeeded (ResultType/ErrorCode 0) and was non-interactive (token/cookie replay). Separate the four residential-proxy IPs (higher FP) from the dedicated hosting IPs (near-certain TP). 2) Contain: revoke sessions and refresh tokens, force password reset + MFA/passkey re-registration, and apply a Conditional Access block on the IPs. 3) Hunt: enumerate every app the session touched, look for bulk file downloads with python-requests/WindowsPowerShell user-agents, and review the inbox for deletion of security/password-reset mail.

Automated bulk cloud data exfiltration via python-requests / PowerShell user-agents AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts high-volume file download/access bursts from M365/SharePoint driven by scripting user-agents (python-requests, WindowsPowerShell) or sourced from UNC6671 exfil IPs — the automated SaaS harvesting stage after SSO compromise. Non-interactive UAs pulling many objects in a short window is the signal. Rationale: Uses the exact automated-tooling user-agents GTIG observed (python-requests/2.28.1, WindowsPowerShell/5.1) plus the three exfil IPs (Tzulo / Hydra Communications) from the article's IOC list; scripting UA + high object count is what distinguishes automated harvesting from human browsing. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/unc6671-targets-financial-services-and-enterprise-cloud-environments
ATT&CKT1530 T1119 T1567.002
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned data-migration or backup tooling (e.g. ShareGate, Mover, AvePoint) using scripted downloads
  • Approved PowerShell (PnP / Microsoft.Graph) automation run by IT for reporting or archival
  • eDiscovery / legal-hold bulk export jobs
  • A developer's python-requests script legitimately syncing SharePoint content
Suppression filter
| where AccountDisplayName !has_any ("svc-migration","sharegate","pnp-automation","ediscovery") and UserAgent !has "Microsoft.Graph"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the scripting UA / exfil IP maps to a sanctioned automation account or an interactive user's hijacked session; quantify distinct files and total volume in the burst. 2) Contain: revoke the session/token, disable the account, and restrict the OAuth app or IP if applicable; snapshot the accessed file list for scoping. 3) Hunt: correlate to a preceding sign-in from UNC6671 infra IPs, check other SaaS apps (Salesforce, Slack, GitHub) for the same session, and review whether security/reset emails were deleted afterward.
CloudAppEvents | where Timestamp > ago(14d) | where ActionType has_any ("FileDownloaded","FileSyncDownloadedFull","FileAccessed","Download") | where UserAgent has_any ("python-requests","WindowsPowerShell/5.1","python-httpx") or IPAddress in ("23.234.75.84","195.140.213.114","195.140.213.115") | summarize Downloads = count(), DistinctObjects = dcount(ObjectName), Apps = make_set(Application, 20), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, UserAgent, bin(Timestamp, 15m) | where Downloads >= 50
OfficeActivity | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d) | where OfficeWorkload in ("SharePoint","OneDrive") | where Operation in ("FileDownloaded","FileSyncDownloadedFull","FileAccessed") | where UserAgent has_any ("python-requests","WindowsPowerShell/5.1") or ClientIP in ("23.234.75.84","195.140.213.114","195.140.213.115") | summarize Ops = count(), DistinctFiles = dcount(ObjectId), Files = make_set(SourceFileName, 20) by UserId, ClientIP, UserAgent, bin(TimeGenerated, 15m) | where Ops >= 50
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count values(Web.dest) as dests from datamodel=Web where (Web.http_user_agent IN ("python-requests*","WindowsPowerShell/5.1*") OR Web.src IN ("23.234.75.84","195.140.213.114","195.140.213.115")) AND Web.action="allowed" by Web.user Web.src Web.http_user_agent _time span=15m | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where count >= 50
| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Web.dest) as dests from datamodel=Web where (Web.http_user_agent IN ("python-requests*","WindowsPowerShell/5.1*") OR Web.src IN ("23.234.75.84","195.140.213.114","195.140.213.115")) AND Web.action="allowed" by Web.user Web.src Web.http_user_agent _time span=15m | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where count >= 50
Rapid multi-cloud SSO application enumeration after single sign-in AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects a single account touching an anomalously large number of distinct SSO-federated cloud apps within a short window — the 'log into the SSO dashboard and reach everything linked' behaviour GTIG/BleepingComputer describe. Behavioural fan-out threshold on distinct app access per user per 10 minutes. Rationale: Directly models the article's 'log into the SSO dashboard, which gives access to all the cloud platforms linked to the account' plus GTIG's noted rapid SaaS access; 8 distinct apps in 10 minutes (threshold tune per tenant) captures automated dashboard sweeps a human rarely produces. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hedge-fund-cyberattacks-tied-to-blackfile-linked-unc6671-extortion-group/ • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/unc6671-targets-financial-services-and-enterprise-cloud-environments
ATT&CKT1526 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Power users / executives who legitimately open many SSO tiles at start of day
  • SSO landing-page pre-authentication that silently issues tokens to multiple apps on login
  • Automated SSO health-check or synthetic-monitoring accounts
  • Onboarding provisioning that grants and immediately exercises many app assignments
Suppression filter
| where AccountUpn !in~ ("svc-monitoring@contoso.com","synthetic-uptime@contoso.com")
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the app list and source IP for the burst; a corporate IP + browser client with a plausible role is likely benign, a UNC6671 infra/residential-proxy IP is not. 2) Contain: if the source IP or velocity is anomalous, revoke sessions/tokens and disable the account pending review. 3) Hunt: pivot to bulk downloads with scripting user-agents from the same session and check for post-access deletion of security-notification emails.
AADSignInEventsBeta | where Timestamp > ago(14d) | where ErrorCode == 0 | summarize AppCount = dcount(ApplicationId), Apps = make_set(Application, 50), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), FirstApp = min(Timestamp), LastApp = max(Timestamp) by AccountUpn, bin(Timestamp, 10m) | where AppCount >= 8
SigninLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d) | where ResultType == 0 | summarize AppCount = dcount(AppId), Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 50), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), FirstApp = min(TimeGenerated), LastApp = max(TimeGenerated) by UserPrincipalName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m) | where AppCount >= 8
source:okta @evt.name:user.authentication.sso @outcome.result:SUCCESS
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true dc(Authentication.app) as app_count values(Authentication.app) as apps values(Authentication.src) as src from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action="success" by Authentication.user _time span=10m | where app_count >= 8
| tstats summariesonly=false dc(Authentication.app) as app_count values(Authentication.app) as apps values(Authentication.src) as src from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action="success" by Authentication.user _time span=10m | where app_count >= 8
Post-compromise deletion of security & password-reset emails from mailbox AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts targeted deletion (soft/hard delete, move-to-deleted) of security-notification and password-reset messages shortly after account compromise — UNC6671's trace-erasure step to stop the victim noticing MFA changes and non-SSO password resets. Subject-keyword + deletion-burst logic. Rationale: Directly encodes the article's 'delete security notifications and password-reset emails from compromised inboxes' and GTIG's detail on erasing MFA-change and password-reset confirmations; subject keywords + a deletion burst separate this from routine mailbox cleanup. Splunk left empty as O365 mailbox-audit has no standard CIM datamodel. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hedge-fund-cyberattacks-tied-to-blackfile-linked-unc6671-extortion-group/ • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/unc6671-targets-financial-services-and-enterprise-cloud-environments
ATT&CKT1070.008 T1070.004
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User with an inbox rule that auto-deletes notification mail from security systems
  • Bulk mailbox cleanup / retention policy purging old alert mail
  • Admin remediating a mailbox after a phishing test
  • User manually clearing MFA/verification-code spam
Suppression filter
| where UserId !in~ ("retention-admin@contoso.com") and ClientIP !startswith "10."
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the deleting principal, source IP, and whether the deletions correlate with a recent anomalous sign-in; inspect the deleted subjects for reset/MFA confirmations. 2) Contain: revoke sessions/tokens, force password + MFA re-registration, and recover deleted items from the dumpster for evidence. 3) Hunt: check for a preceding sign-in from UNC6671 infra IPs, non-SSO app password resets initiated by the account, and bulk SaaS downloads from the same session.
CloudAppEvents | where Timestamp > ago(14d) | where Application in~ ("Microsoft Exchange Online","Exchange Online") | where ActionType has_any ("SoftDelete","HardDelete","MoveToDeletedItems","Delete message") | summarize Deletes = count(), Subjects = make_set(ObjectName, 25), Sources = make_set(IPAddress, 10), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, bin(Timestamp, 10m) | where Deletes >= 3
OfficeActivity | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d) | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange" | where Operation in ("SoftDelete","HardDelete","MoveToDeletedItems") | where Subject has_any ("password reset","reset your password","security alert","unusual sign-in","new sign-in","MFA","multi-factor","multifactor","passkey","verification code","security info","was added","did you just") | summarize Deletes = count(), Subjects = make_set(Subject, 25), Clients = make_set(ClientIP, 10) by UserId, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m) | where Deletes >= 3

  selection_subj:

Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent

                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",

| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High

Swiss government SharePoint breach compromised 200 accounts

BleepingComputer
2026-08-06 8 use cases 2 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Switzerland's federal IT office says hackers exploited vulnerabilities to breach its Microsoft SharePoint servers and compromised approximately 200 accounts. [...]

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Anomalous POST to SharePoint ToolPane/_trust exploit endpoints (CVE-2026-50522/56164)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] SharePoint IIS worker (w3wp.exe) spawning command interpreter — ToolShell RCE
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] SharePoint MachineKey / web.config credential theft via w3wp child process · [LLM] Webshell/.aspx written into SharePoint LAYOUTS by w3wp.exe (ToolShell persistence)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Anomalous POST to SharePoint ToolPane/_trust exploit endpoints (CVE-2026-50522/56164) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound POST requests to the SharePoint endpoints abused by the July 2026 patch-Tuesday chain — /_layouts/15/ToolPane.aspx and the /_trust/default.aspx WS-Federation sign-in path where CVE-2026-50522 delivers a BinaryFormatter SecurityContextToken cookie. Surfaces the first foothold on internet-facing SharePoint servers. Rationale: Uses the two concrete exploit endpoints corroborated for this chain — ToolPane.aspx (CVE-2026-56164 EoP path) and /_trust/default.aspx (CVE-2026-50522 WS-Federation deserialization). Referer and low status codes help separate exploit probes from legit editing. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/critical-sharepoint-rce-flaw-exploited-to-steal-machine-keys/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/22/sharepoint-cve-2026-50522-exploited/ • https://www.trellix.com/blogs/research/toolshell-unleashed-decoding-the-sharepoint-attack-chain/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate SharePoint page authors editing web-part zones hit ToolPane.aspx from internal IPs
  • Federated SSO / ADFS traffic legitimately posting to /_trust/default.aspx
  • Vulnerability scanners (Qualys/Tenable) probing SharePoint endpoints
  • Load-balancer / uptime monitors POSTing health checks
  • SharePoint farm timer jobs generating internal POSTs
Suppression filter
| where NOT (cidr_match("10.0.0.0/8", cIP) OR cidr_match("192.168.0.0/16", cIP))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the cIP is external/untrusted and correlate the timestamp with w3wp.exe child-process activity (UC2) on the same Computer. Pull the full csUriQuery and User-Agent. 2) Contain: block external access to SharePoint (as BIT did), and firewall the source IP; snapshot the server for forensics. 3) Hunt: pivot to any w3wp.exe→cmd/powershell spawns, reads of web.config/machine.config, and newly written .aspx files under the LAYOUTS directory in the following hours.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csMethod == "POST"
| where csUriStem has_any ("/_layouts/15/ToolPane.aspx", "/_trust/default.aspx") or csUriStem endswith "ToolPane.aspx"
| where scStatus in ("200","302","401","500")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csReferer, scStatus, csUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SharePoint IIS worker (w3wp.exe) spawning command interpreter — ToolShell RCE AIExploitation High
Alerts when the SharePoint/IIS worker process w3wp.exe spawns cmd.exe, powershell.exe or other interpreters/LOLBins. This parent→child chain is the execution signature of CVE-2026-50522 RCE and does not occur in normal SharePoint operation. Rationale: w3wp.exe (SharePoint app-pool worker) spawning an interpreter is the highest-fidelity execution signal for this chain — corroborated across Splunk, Trellix and Anomali ToolShell writeups as abnormal in legitimate SharePoint operation. Named parent/child binaries make it alert-grade. Cross-checked against: • https://www.splunk.com/en_us/blog/security/sharepoint-exploits-and-the-hidden-threat-of-iis-module-persistence.html • https://www.anomali.com/blog/detecting-the-toolshell-sharepoint-exploit • https://www.trellix.com/blogs/research/toolshell-unleashed-decoding-the-sharepoint-attack-chain/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.001 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SharePoint installation/patching (PSConfig) transiently running under an app-pool identity
  • Admin-authored SharePoint timer jobs or custom web parts shelling out
  • Health-analyzer or monitoring solutions invoking scripts via the worker process
  • Antivirus/EDR remediation spawning under w3wp context
  • Custom in-house SharePoint solutions that legitimately call certutil/PowerShell
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("PSConfig","wsadmin","stsadm") and InitiatingProcessIntegrityLevel == "System")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child ProcessCommandLine — decode any -EncodedCommand, look for download/machine-key strings. Correlate with UC1 inbound POSTs on the same host/time. 2) Contain: isolate the SharePoint server from the network and block external SharePoint access; suspend the app pool. Because machine keys may be stolen, plan key rotation + server reinstall (BIT reinstalled affected servers). 3) Hunt: search for web.config/machine.config reads (UC3), dropped .aspx webshells (UC4), and forged-token sign-ins across the ~200 potentially affected accounts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe","rundll32.exe","csc.exe","certutil.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessIntegrityLevel, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\w3wp.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\mshta.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\rundll32.exe","\\csc.exe","\\certutil.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SharePoint MachineKey / web.config credential theft via w3wp child process AIInstallation High
Detects the credential-access step of CVE-2026-50522 where post-RCE code reads SharePoint ValidationKey/DecryptionKey material from web.config or machine.config to forge __VIEWSTATE/auth tokens. Fires on an interpreter spawned by w3wp.exe whose command line references machine-key config or key fields. Rationale: Targets the exact post-exploitation objective corroborated by BleepingComputer/HelpNetSecurity/watchTowr for CVE-2026-50522: stealing SharePoint machine keys (ValidationKey/DecryptionKey) from web.config/machine.config to forge tokens. The w3wp parent + key-material string combo is very high fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/critical-sharepoint-rce-flaw-exploited-to-steal-machine-keys/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/22/sharepoint-cve-2026-50522-exploited/ • https://www.trellix.com/blogs/research/toolshell-unleashed-decoding-the-sharepoint-attack-chain/
ATT&CKT1552.004 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SharePoint patch/config operations (PSConfig, Update-SPMachineKey) legitimately touching machine keys
  • Admin PowerShell reading web.config for troubleshooting under the app-pool account
  • Farm build automation that rotates machine keys
  • Backup jobs enumerating config files
  • Custom deployment scripts referencing web.config paths
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Update-SPMachineKey","PSConfig") and AccountName endswith "$")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full command line and determine whether ValidationKey/DecryptionKey values were read or written out (base64/file redirection). Confirm the parent w3wp and any preceding UC1 POST. 2) Contain: treat machine keys as compromised — isolate the server, rotate/regenerate SharePoint machine keys across the farm, and force password resets on affected accounts (BIT reset ~200). 3) Hunt: because stolen keys enable forged tokens surviving patching, hunt for anomalous authenticated SharePoint sessions and __VIEWSTATE replays after the reset, and plan server reinstall.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("machineKey","ValidationKey","DecryptionKey","web.config","machine.config")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\w3wp.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\cmd.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\wscript.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any ("machineKey","ValidationKey","DecryptionKey","web.config","machine.config")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Webshell/.aspx written into SharePoint LAYOUTS by w3wp.exe (ToolShell persistence) AIInstallation Medium
Detects the SharePoint worker process writing new .aspx/.ashx files into the SharePoint TEMPLATE\LAYOUTS or web-root directories — the webshell/key-exfil persistence pattern (e.g. spinstall0.aspx) used in the ToolShell chain to drop a page that returns the stolen machine keys or maintains RCE access. Rationale: The SharePoint worker writing a fresh .aspx into LAYOUTS (the spinstall0.aspx-style key-exfil/webshell drop documented in ToolShell) is a rare, high-signal persistence event that maps directly to this campaign's machine-key theft and post-patch access retention. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trellix.com/blogs/research/toolshell-unleashed-decoding-the-sharepoint-attack-chain/ • https://www.sygnia.co/threat-reports-and-advisories/on-prem-sharepoint-toolshell-backdoor-advisory/ • https://www.anomali.com/blog/detecting-the-toolshell-sharepoint-exploit
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SharePoint patching/PSConfig deploying legitimate new LAYOUTS pages
  • Installation of a SharePoint solution package (WSP) that provisions .aspx files
  • Farm feature activation writing application pages
  • Third-party SharePoint add-in deployment
  • Developer publishing a custom application page during a maintenance window
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("PSConfig","stsadm","Install-SPSolution"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: retrieve and read the dropped .aspx — look for code that outputs ValidationKey/DecryptionKey, accepts commands, or reflects __VIEWSTATE. Note file hash and creation time; correlate with UC1/UC2/UC3. 2) Contain: remove/quarantine the file, isolate the server, and treat machine keys as stolen (rotate keys, reset affected account passwords, reinstall server per BIT's remediation). 3) Hunt: enumerate all recently-created .aspx/.ashx across the farm, check IIS logs for GETs to the dropped filename from external IPs, and review authenticated sessions for forged-token reuse post-patch.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where FileName endswith ".aspx" or FileName endswith ".ashx"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\TEMPLATE\LAYOUTS", @"\16\TEMPLATE", @"\web server extensions", @"\wwwroot")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where ActingProcessName endswith "\\w3wp.exe"
| where TargetFileName endswith ".aspx" or TargetFileName endswith ".ashx"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("\\TEMPLATE\\LAYOUTS", "\\16\\TEMPLATE", "\\web server extensions", "\\wwwroot")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents

New Zapscape KVM Flaw Could Let Privileged L1 Guest Code Escape to Linux Hosts

The Hacker News
2026-08-06 7 use cases 3 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Zapscape, a new Linux kernel vulnerability, could allow an attacker with kernel privileges inside an L1 guest virtual machine (VM) to escape KVM isolation and execute code on the host. The risk applies when nested virtualization is exposed to untrusted guests. The flaw is tracked as&nbsp;CVE-2026-64561&nbsp;and affects KVM/x86's shadow memory management unit (MMU), which manages shadow page

—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Zapscape KVM escape artifact: root-owned /Zapscape file created on host · [LLM] Exposure hunt: KVM hosts vulnerable to Zapscape (CVE-2026-64561) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Zapscape KVM escape artifact: root-owned /Zapscape file created on host AIExploitation High
Hunts the definitive success marker of the Zapscape (CVE-2026-64561) KVM VM-escape PoC: a file literally named /Zapscape created at filesystem root, owned by root (uid=0, mode 0644), on a KVM hypervisor. Creation of this exact path by the host kernel confirms an L1 guest escaped shadow-MMU isolation and executed code with host root. Rationale: The PoC's own output string confirms it creates /Zapscape at root (uid=0, mode 0644) as its exploitation proof; a file with that exact name at filesystem root is not a legitimate artifact, making it a near-zero-FP success marker. Filename and behaviour cross-checked against the author's GitHub PoC (V4bel/Zapscape). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/V4bel/Zapscape • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/new-zapscape-kvm-flaw-could-let.html
ATT&CKT1611 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or red team running the public Zapscape PoC in a sanctioned lab
  • Blue team detonating the exploit to validate this very detection
  • A sysadmin manually running touch /Zapscape while testing the detection rule
  • Honeypot / deception host intentionally seeded with the marker file
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("labadmin","secops-test") and DeviceName !has "sandbox"
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm the host is a KVM hypervisor exposing nested virtualization to guests; pull file owner/mode (expect root:root 0644) and the InitiatingProcess — a kernel/kworker context strongly implies genuine escape, a user shell implies manual/test creation. 2) Contain: Treat as full host compromise at kernel-root — isolate the hypervisor from the network, snapshot memory/disk for forensics, and quarantine/pause co-resident tenant VMs since any could be the origin guest. 3) Hunt: Identify the running kernel version vs fixed builds (6.6.148/6.12.101/6.18.42/7.1.6), review recent guest-side kernel module loads, and check for follow-on host root activity (new accounts, cron, SSH keys).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName =~ "Zapscape"
| where FolderPath in~ ("/Zapscape", "/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, FolderPath, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFilePath =~ "/Zapscape" or TargetFileName =~ "Zapscape"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Exposure hunt: KVM hosts vulnerable to Zapscape (CVE-2026-64561) AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces Linux hosts still carrying the Zapscape shadow-MMU use-after-free (CVE-2026-64561) so KVM hypervisors that expose nested virtualization to untrusted guests can be prioritised for patching to a fixed kernel (6.6.148, 6.12.101, 6.18.42, 7.1.6, or 7.2-rc5+). Article-specific exposure detection tied to the assigned CVE. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete CVE identifier (CVE-2026-64561) and enumerated fixed kernel versions to drive a targeted exposure hunt; joining to DeviceInfo flags internet-facing/multi-tenant hypervisors that carry the real escape risk. CVE and fixed versions corroborated against the PoC repo and vendor tracking. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/V4bel/Zapscape • https://cybernews.com/security/januscape-linux-kvm-vulnerability-exposes-cloud/
ATT&CKT1611 T1068
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Host already patched but TVM inventory cache is stale (lag between patch and rescan)
  • Red Hat/vendor backported the fix without bumping the upstream version string, so version-string scanners may mis-flag a fixed host
  • Desktop/non-hypervisor Linux hosts where nested virt is not exposed to untrusted guests (vulnerable but low real-world risk)
  • VM guests rather than the KVM host itself appearing in results
Response runbook
1) Triage: Filter results to actual KVM hypervisors that expose nested virtualization to untrusted/multi-tenant guests — these are the true blast-radius hosts; deprioritise standalone desktops. 2) Contain: For internet-facing or multi-tenant hosts, schedule emergency patching to a fixed kernel (6.6.148/6.12.101/6.18.42/7.1.6/7.2-rc5+) or vendor backport; as interim mitigation, disable nested virtualization exposure to untrusted guests. 3) Hunt: On each exposed host, retro-hunt for the /Zapscape artifact and anomalous guest kernel-module loads to rule out prior exploitation before patch.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
