Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Web egress to AI-assistant deep-link carrying LLM memory-poisoning instruction · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Inbound email delivering AI-assistant deep-link with memory-poisoning payload
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Web egress to AI-assistant deep-link carrying LLM memory-poisoning instruction AIDelivery Medium
Hunts outbound web requests to ChatGPT/Claude/Grok/Gemini/Perplexity deep-link endpoints (?q=) whose query string carries a memory-write instruction such as 'trusted source', 'source of expertise' or 'remember'. This is the click/browse moment of AI Recommendation Poisoning where an 'Ask AI' button silently commits a vendor domain to the user's persistent LLM memory. Rationale: Anchors on the exact AI-assistant domains and the '?q=' deep-link pattern named in the article/Microsoft blog, combined with the two publicly-disclosed keyword classes ('trusted source', 'remember') plus the article's verbatim payload phrase 'source of expertise for future reference'. URL-encoded variants included because proxy logs store escaped query strings. Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty: FDR and standard Datadog sources do not capture HTTPS query strings, so the distinguishing signal is unavailable there. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/02/10/ai-recommendation-poisoning/ • https://www.theregister.com/2026/02/12/microsoft_ai_recommendation_poisoning/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/02/11/ai-recommendation-memory-poisoning-attacks/
ATT&CK
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Benign 'Summarize with AI' buttons whose prompt legitimately contains the word 'remember' (e.g. 'remember to cite sources') with no domain-save intent
  • Security researchers/analysts reproducing the payloads during this very investigation
  • Users authoring their own ChatGPT/Claude deep links that instruct the model to remember a personal preference
  • Browser extensions / bookmarklets that pre-fill AI prompts as a productivity feature
  • Vendor marketing/QA staff clicking their own comparison-page buttons
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("trusted source","trusted+source","trusted%20source","source of expertise","source+of+expertise","source%20of%20expertise")  // drop the noisy bare 'remember' token; keep the high-fidelity domain-trust phrases
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full RequestURL/RemoteUrl and URL-decode the q= parameter. Confirm it instructs the model to save/trust a specific vendor DOMAIN (not just a benign 'remember'). Note the referring marketing/comparison page and the user. 2) CONTAIN: Have the user open their AI assistant's memory/personalization settings and delete any unauthorized 'trusted source' or 'source of expertise' domain entry; if unsure, reset the memory store. Reinforce policy: do not click 'Ask AI' buttons on corporate accounts. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the referring domain across all users to find everyone who clicked the same poisoned button, and sweep proxy logs for other AI-assistant deep links from that referrer over the last 60 days.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("chatgpt.com","claude.ai","grok.com","gemini.google.com","perplexity.ai")
| where RemoteUrl has "q="
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("trusted source","trusted+source","trusted%20source","source of expertise","source+of+expertise","source%20of%20expertise","remember")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","arc.exe","iexplore.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RequestURL has_any ("chatgpt.com","claude.ai","grok.com","gemini.google.com","perplexity.ai")
| where RequestURL has "q="
| where RequestURL has_any ("trusted source","trusted+source","trusted%20source","source of expertise","source+of+expertise","source%20of%20expertise","remember")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: AI-Assistant Deep-Link Carrying LLM Memory-Poisoning Instruction
id: a3f1c2e4-9b7d-4e2a-8f6c-1d2e3f4a5b6c
description: Detects outbound web requests to AI-assistant deep-link endpoints whose query string contains a persistent-memory write instruction (AI Recommendation Poisoning).
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/ai-recommendation-poisoning-how-ask-ai.html
  - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/02/10/ai-recommendation-poisoning/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/06
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - atlas.aml_t0051
  - atlas.aml_t0080
logsource:
  category: proxy
detection:
  domain:
    c-uri|contains:
      - 'chatgpt.com'
      - 'claude.ai'
      - 'grok.com'
      - 'gemini.google.com'
      - 'perplexity.ai'
  deeplink:
    c-uri|contains: 'q='
  payload:
    c-uri|contains:
      - 'trusted source'
      - 'trusted+source'
      - 'trusted%20source'
      - 'source of expertise'
      - 'source+of+expertise'
      - 'source%20of%20expertise'
      - 'remember'

level: medium
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*chatgpt.com*" OR Web.url="*claude.ai*" OR Web.url="*grok.com*" OR Web.url="*gemini.google.com*" OR Web.url="*perplexity.ai*") AND Web.url="*q=*" AND (Web.url="*trusted*source*" OR Web.url="*trusted+source*" OR Web.url="*trusted%20source*" OR Web.url="*source*of*expertise*" OR Web.url="*source+of+expertise*" OR Web.url="*remember*") by Web.src Web.user Web.dest Web.url Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*chatgpt.com*" OR Web.url="*claude.ai*" OR Web.url="*grok.com*" OR Web.url="*gemini.google.com*" OR Web.url="*perplexity.ai*") AND Web.url="*q=*" AND (Web.url="*trusted*source*" OR Web.url="*trusted+source*" OR Web.url="*trusted%20source*" OR Web.url="*source*of*expertise*" OR Web.url="*source+of+expertise*" OR Web.url="*remember*") by Web.src Web.user Web.dest Web.url Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Inbound email delivering AI-assistant deep-link with memory-poisoning payload AIInstallation Medium
Hunts delivered inbound email containing a link to an AI-assistant deep-link (?q=) whose query string carries a persistent-memory write instruction. Catches the AI Recommendation Poisoning payload at the mail-delivery layer before the recipient clicks, treating the memory-manipulation link the way Microsoft advises treating credential-harvesting links. Rationale: Reuses the same article-grounded AI-assistant domains, '?q=' deep-link pattern and disclosed memory-write phrases, but pivots on EmailUrlInfo joined to inbound EmailEvents to catch the payload at delivery — a genuinely different log source and phase from the web-egress UC. Sentinel/Sigma/Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty: EmailUrlInfo (Defender for O365 URL extraction) has no clean equivalent on those platforms in this tenant, and the detection is a cross-table join so Sigma's single-event shape does not fit. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/02/10/ai-recommendation-poisoning/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/02/microsoft-finds-summarize-with-ai.html
ATT&CK
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate newsletters/marketing mail embedding benign 'Summarize with AI' share buttons that happen to include the word 'remember'
  • Internal red-team / awareness phishing simulations replaying this payload
  • A colleague forwarding a legitimately-authored ChatGPT/Claude deep link containing a personal 'remember my preference' instruction
  • Vendor product-comparison emails whose 'Ask AI' link uses 'source of expertise' as legitimate GEO marketing
Suppression filter
| where Url has_any ("trusted source","trusted+source","trusted%20source","source of expertise","source+of+expertise","source%20of%20expertise")  // drop bare 'remember'; retain explicit domain-trust instructions
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: URL-decode the q= parameter from EmailUrlInfo and confirm it instructs the model to save/trust a specific domain; check DeliveryAction/DeliveryLocation to see if it reached the inbox, then check UrlClickEvents for that NetworkMessageId to see if the recipient actually clicked. 2) CONTAIN: If clicked, direct the user to purge unauthorized 'trusted source'/'source of expertise' entries from their AI memory (or reset it); soft-delete/quarantine the message for all recipients via Explorer. 3) HUNT: Cluster on SenderFromAddress and SenderMailFromDomain to find the full campaign, and cross-reference the embedded vendor domain against the web-egress UC to see who browsed the same payload on the open web.
let AiDomains = dynamic(["chatgpt.com","claude.ai","grok.com","gemini.google.com","perplexity.ai"]);
let MemPhrases = dynamic(["trusted source","trusted+source","trusted%20source","source of expertise","source+of+expertise","source%20of%20expertise","remember"]);
EmailUrlInfo
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Url has_any (AiDomains)
| where Url has "q="
| where Url has_any (MemPhrases)
| join kind=inner (
    EmailEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"

  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, Url, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation
| order by Timestamp desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] AI resource key creation paired with logging/alert teardown in cloud control plane
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound traffic to known AI token-jacking transfer-station infrastructure (Unit42 IPs) · [LLM] Transfer-station client fingerprint: Go-http-client/2.0,gzip(gfe) user-agent in web egress · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Outbound traffic to known AI token-jacking transfer-station infrastructure (Unit42 IPs) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts corporate host or cloud egress to the four IP addresses Unit 42 tied to malicious AI API calls from gray-market 'transfer stations' (new-api/one-api proxies) abusing stolen tokens. A connection from inside the environment to any of these IPs indicates either the transfer-station infrastructure being reached or a compromised host relaying stolen-token traffic. Rationale: Uses the four exact IPs from Unit 42's IOC table ('Malicious API calls'). IP-literal egress match is high-fidelity and article-specific; corroboration of the campaign economy (LLMjacking/transfer stations) via KPMG and Zscaler, though the IPs themselves are single-sourced to Unit 42. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/ai-token-jacking/ • https://kpmg.com/us/en/articles/2026/ai-emerging-threat.html • https://www.zscaler.com/blogs/security-research/shai-hulud-v2-poses-risk-npm-supply-chain
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Cloud-hosted app on 3.235.0.0/16 (AWS us-east-1) shares an IP range with legitimate SaaS — verify the exact /32
  • Threat-intel enrichment or sandbox VMs deliberately connecting to flagged IPs
  • A security researcher in the org validating the IOCs
  • Shared-hosting IP later reassigned to a benign tenant (IOC decay — confirm timestamp vs. article publish date)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe") and InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the internal src host/user and the process that made the connection; confirm the dst is the exact /32 and note bytes transferred (large volume = active token relay). 2) CONTAIN: Block the four IPs at egress/firewall, isolate the source host, and immediately rotate/revoke any AI provider API keys reachable from that host. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the same host for infostealer/npm-worm artifacts (Shai-Hulud/Miasma), search for the Go-http-client UA in proxy logs, and audit AI-provider consoles for unauthorized key creation and disabled billing alerts.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("3.235.109.125","116.105.166.148","172.96.142.186","38.46.219.166")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Connections=count() by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by LastSeen desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in ("3.235.109.125","116.105.166.148","172.96.142.186","38.46.219.166")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Count=count() by SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, DeviceVendor, RequestClientApplication
| order by LastSeen desc

Transfer-station client fingerprint: Go-http-client/2.0,gzip(gfe) user-agent in web egress AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the exact HTTP User-Agent string Unit 42 tied to malicious AI API calls made by transfer-station proxies (new-api/one-api). Its appearance in outbound web/proxy telemetry — especially toward AI provider API endpoints — flags stolen-token abuse or a compromised host acting as an API relay. Rationale: Uses the verbatim User-Agent from Unit 42's IOC table. The 'gzip(gfe)' suffix (Google Frontend) on a Go default client is an unusual fingerprint for corporate egress; medium confidence because bare Go clients are legit, so pair with AI-API destination domains during triage. Defender/Falcon left empty — their network telemetry does not carry the HTTP User-Agent header. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/ai-token-jacking/ • https://kpmg.com/us/en/articles/2026/ai-emerging-threat.html
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate internal Go microservices/CI jobs using the default net/http client that traverse a GFE-fronted API
  • Go-based SDKs calling Google/GCP services (the gzip(gfe) marker comes from Google Frontend)
  • Monitoring/uptime agents written in Go
  • Homegrown API integrations that never set a custom UA
Suppression filter
| where DstHostname has_any ("openai","anthropic","googleapis","generativelanguage","api.x.ai","deepseek")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Enumerate the destination domains for this UA — legitimate internal Go services should hit known APIs; hits to LLM provider endpoints (OpenAI/Anthropic/Gemini) with this UA are the true positive. 2) CONTAIN: If the destination is an AI API and the source is not a sanctioned service, revoke the API keys used from that host and block the flow. 3) HUNT: Correlate the source with UC1 IP hits and with any recent npm install activity (Shai-Hulud/Miasma) or infostealer detections on the host.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent has "Go-http-client/2.0,gzip(gfe)"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Requests=count(), Domains=make_set(DstHostname, 20) by SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by Requests desc

AI resource key creation paired with logging/alert teardown in cloud control plane AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the developer-account abuse Unit 42 lists: attackers who steal privileged AI/cloud credentials then create new API keys and disable usage alerts/logging so token theft stays invisible until the bill arrives. Detects the same principal regenerating/creating keys on an AI (Cognitive Services / Bedrock) resource while deleting diagnostic or model-invocation logging in a short window. Rationale: Directly operationalizes the article's four enumerated developer-account abuses ('Creating new API keys', 'Provisioning models', 'Disabling critical usage alerts and logging') as concrete Azure Cognitive Services and AWS Bedrock control-plane operations. The key-creation + logging-delete combo within a window is the article-specific behavioral signal, not a generic admin action. Defender/Falcon/Sigma left empty — this is cloud audit telemetry not in Defender XDR endpoint tables, and it's a multi-op correlation unsuited to single-event Sigma. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/ai-token-jacking/ • https://kpmg.com/us/en/articles/2026/ai-emerging-threat.html
ATT&CKT1098.001 T1562.008 T1078.004
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Platform team rotating Cognitive Services keys during scheduled secret rotation
  • IaC/Terraform runs that recreate diagnostic settings (delete then re-add) in the same window
  • Legitimate model deployment change alongside a logging config refresh
  • AWS admin reconfiguring Bedrock model-invocation logging destination (delete + re-put)
  • Break-glass/service-principal automation that legitimately manages keys and logs together
Suppression filter
| where Caller !endswith "terraform" and Caller !has "iac-" and CallerIpAddress != ""
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the Caller/CallerIpAddress is expected — check whether the same principal both created/rotated a key AND deleted logging (benign rotation re-adds logging; malicious tears it down). Review the source IP against UC1 IOCs and geolocation. 2) CONTAIN: Revoke the newly created/regenerated key, re-enable diagnostic/model-invocation logging, and force credential reset on the developer/service account. 3) HUNT: Query AI provider usage/billing for a token-consumption spike, and trace how the account credential was obtained (infostealer, phishing, or npm worm) on the developer's endpoint.

| where Ops has "Microsoft.Insights/diagnosticSettings/delete" and (Ops has "Microsoft.CognitiveServices/accounts/regenerateKey/action" or Ops has "Microsoft.CognitiveServices/accounts/deployments/write")
| order by LastSeen desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName

// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Attackers Compile khunt Inside Oracle to Turn SQL Injection Into Windows SYSTEM Access

The Hacker News
2026-08-06 12 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Attackers broke into an organization's Oracle database through a SQL injection flaw in a public-facing web application, then installed a post-exploitation toolkit without writing an executable to disk. They fed Java source code to the database, let Oracle compile it into stored schema objects, and ran commands from inside the database engine. Huntress, which tracks the toolkit as khunt,

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Inbound requests from khunt attacker IP 178.162.151.229 / Oracle Java SQLi tokens against public web app · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Oracle DB engine (oracle.exe) spawning cmd.exe / LOLBins — khunt KhuntCmd OS execution · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Attackers Compile khunt Inside Oracle to Turn SQL Injection Into Windows SYSTEM
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Oracle audit/SQL logs — KHUNT% schema objects and CREATE JAVA SOURCE / dbms_java
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] SAM/SECURITY/SYSTEM hive dump to F:\Oracle via reg save / esentutl — khunt credential theft · [LLM] khunt on-disk artifacts — khunt*.hiv, khunttasks.txt written under F:\Oracle
Oracle DB engine (oracle.exe) spawning cmd.exe / LOLBins — khunt KhuntCmd OS execution AIExploitation High
Hunts the core khunt behaviour: the Oracle database process compiling a Java source object and using Runtime.exec to spawn OS command interpreters. In this incident 'cmd.exe /c whoami' returned SYSTEM. An Oracle listener/instance process spawning cmd.exe, powershell.exe, reg.exe, esentutl.exe, tasklist.exe or whoami.exe is not normal DB activity and indicates in-database code execution. Rationale: Parent oracle.exe -> cmd.exe/whoami is the confirmed khunt signature (Huntress observed 'cmd.exe /c whoami' returning SYSTEM). Oracle never legitimately spawns whoami/reg/esentutl, making the parent-child pair very high fidelity. Cross-checked Huntress blog (confirms oracle.exe parent) and BleepingComputer. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/khunt-malware-sql-injection-oracle • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-run-khunt-post-exploitation-toolkit-from-oracle-database/ • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4206096/attackers-hid-malware-inside-oracle-database-after-sql-injection-breach.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DBMS_SCHEDULER external jobs legitimately spawning cmd.exe via extjob.exe/oracle.exe for scheduled OS tasks
  • DBA running RMAN backup scripts that shell out to OS utilities from the Oracle service context
  • Monitoring/APM agents injected into the Oracle process invoking tasklist or ipconfig
  • Oracle patching (opatch) launching cmd.exe during maintenance windows
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\jobs\",@"\opatch\") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("extjob","rman","opatch"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full child command line and the SHA256; confirm whether it is whoami/reg/esentutl (attack) vs a known DBMS_SCHEDULER external job. Check ProcessIntegrityLevel — SYSTEM strongly favours true positive. 2) Contain: isolate the DB host, kill the child process tree, and disable the Oracle account's CREATE PROCEDURE / JAVA privileges; block 178.162.151.229 at perimeter. 3) Hunt: query Oracle DBA_OBJECTS/audit for object names LIKE 'KHUNT%' and any CREATE JAVA SOURCE; look on-host for F:\Oracle\khunt*.hiv and khunttasks.txt.
DeviceProcessEvents

| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","reg.exe","esentutl.exe","tasklist.exe","whoami.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","nltest.exe","ipconfig.exe")

SAM/SECURITY/SYSTEM hive dump to F:\Oracle via reg save / esentutl — khunt credential theft AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the credential-access stage where the SYSTEM-level Oracle foothold copied registry hives to disk. Attackers used reg.exe save and esentutl.exe to write SAM, SECURITY and SYSTEM hives to F:\Oracle as khuntSAM.hiv/khuntSECURITY.hiv/khuntSYSTEM.hiv. Detects the hive-export command lines and the khunt staging filenames. Rationale: Combines the generic hive-dump command shape (reg save HKLM\SAM|SECURITY|SYSTEM, esentutl copy) with the incident-specific khunt*.hiv filenames and F:\Oracle staging path confirmed on the Huntress blog — the filename tokens make this near-zero FP versus a bare reg-save rule. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/khunt-malware-sql-injection-oracle • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-run-khunt-post-exploitation-toolkit-from-oracle-database/
ATT&CKT1003.002 T1003.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate IR/forensics tooling (KAPE, velociraptor) exporting SAM/SYSTEM hives during an authorised collection
  • Backup software using esentutl for ESE database maintenance (not hive files)
  • Sysadmin exporting a registry hive for troubleshooting to a non-khunt path
  • Domain migration tooling copying SYSTEM hive
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("kape.exe","velociraptor.exe") or FolderPath has_any (@"\KAPE\",@"\Velociraptor\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the destination path — F:\Oracle or a khunt* filename is decisive; check the parent chain traces back to oracle.exe. 2) Contain: treat all local + cached domain credentials on the host as compromised, force password resets (incl. the Oracle service and any local admin), isolate the host and delete the staged .hiv files after acquiring copies. 3) Hunt: search for exfil of the .hiv files (large outbound to 178.162.151.229), and pivot to KhuntHash output — Oracle SYS.USER$ dumps written to disk.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("reg.exe","esentutl.exe","powershell.exe","cmd.exe")
| where (ProcessCommandLine has "save" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("HKLM\\SAM","HKLM\\SECURITY","HKLM\\SYSTEM"))
     or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("khuntSAM","khuntSECURITY","khuntSYSTEM","khunt_SECURITY")
     or (ProcessCommandLine has "esentutl" and ProcessCommandLine has @"F:\Oracle")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessIntegrityLevel
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\reg.exe","\\esentutl.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\cmd.exe")
| where (CommandLine has "save" and CommandLine has_any ("HKLM\\SAM","HKLM\\SECURITY","HKLM\\SYSTEM"))
     or CommandLine has_any ("khuntSAM","khuntSECURITY","khuntSYSTEM","khunt_SECURITY")
     or (CommandLine has "esentutl" and CommandLine has "F:\\Oracle")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Inbound requests from khunt attacker IP 178.162.151.229 / Oracle Java SQLi tokens against public web app AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the initial-access vector: SQL injection in a public-facing Java web app's autocomplete search field, abused to reach an Oracle DB over JDBC. Leads with the confirmed attacker IP 178.162.151.229 and Oracle-Java injection markers (CREATE JAVA SOURCE, dbms_java, runtime.exec, KHUNT) in web request query strings, plus endpoint connections to that IP. Rationale: 178.162.151.229 is the request-source IP named by Huntress and independently reported by BleepingComputer (second-source confirmed, so shipped). Oracle-Java injection tokens (CREATE JAVA SOURCE, dbms_java, runtime.exec) are the exact primitives the article says the attacker used to author Java sources — high-signal in a web query string. Defender lacks HTTP-request tables so the endpoint variant pivots on DeviceNetworkEvents to the IP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/khunt-malware-sql-injection-oracle • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-run-khunt-post-exploitation-toolkit-from-oracle-database/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security scanner / pentest hitting the same app with Oracle SQLi payloads during an authorised assessment
  • WAF or DAST tooling generating csUriQuery entries containing 'dbms_java' as test payloads
  • Shared NAT/proxy egress causing an unrelated host to appear to talk to the IP
  • Threat-intel feed enrichment tools resolving/probing the IP
Suppression filter
| where csUserAgent !has_any ("sqlmap","Nessus","Qualys","Burp","acunetix")
Response runbook
1) Triage: for IP hits confirm direction (inbound to the web tier = exploitation attempt); for token hits inspect csUriStem to identify the autocomplete/search endpoint and whether scStatus 200 indicates success. 2) Contain: block 178.162.151.229 at the WAF/firewall, take the vulnerable search endpoint offline or enable WAF SQLi rules, rotate the app's JDBC/Oracle service credentials. 3) Hunt: pivot to the DB host for oracle.exe child processes (UC1) and KHUNT% objects; review IIS logs for the same source ASN over a wider window.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "178.162.151.229" or LocalIP == "178.162.151.229"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, LocalIP, LocalPort, RemoteIP, RemotePort,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where cIP == "178.162.151.229"
   or csUriQuery has_any ("CREATE JAVA SOURCE","CREATE%20JAVA","dbms_java","DBMS_JAVA","runtime.exec","KHUNT")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, csUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

khunt on-disk artifacts — khunt*.hiv, khunttasks.txt written under F:\Oracle AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the toolkit's file-staging footprint independent of which binary wrote it. khunt wrote credential hives (khuntSAM.hiv, khuntSECURITY.hiv, khuntSYSTEM.hiv, khunt_SECURITY.hiv), a service-enumeration dump (khunttasks.txt from tasklist /svc), and KhuntHash password output — all under F:\Oracle. Any file whose name begins 'khunt' is a direct IOC. Rationale: The literal filenames (khuntSAM.hiv, khunttasks.txt, khunt_SECURITY.hiv, all under F:\Oracle) are confirmed on the Huntress blog and are unique enough that a 'khunt' filename prefix is effectively a signature with negligible FP — a different log-source pivot (file events) from the process-based UCs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/khunt-malware-sql-injection-oracle
ATT&CKT1074.001 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal tool or user coincidentally named with a 'khunt' prefix (rare)
  • Restore/analysis of the incident's own artifacts by IR staff on the same host
  • Security team deliberately re-creating IOC files to test this detection
  • Backup software copying the staged .hiv files to another path
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the writing process (InitiatingProcessFileName) — expect reg.exe/esentutl.exe/powershell parented to oracle.exe; capture file hashes and sizes before touching. 2) Contain: preserve then remove the staged files, isolate the host, and treat any SAM/SECURITY/SYSTEM hives as leaked credentials requiring resets. 3) Hunt: search all Oracle hosts for the 'khunt' filename prefix and for KHUNT% database objects; check outbound transfer of these files to 178.162.151.229.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName startswith "khunt"
   or FileName in~ ("khunttasks.txt","khuntSAM.hiv","khuntSECURITY.hiv","khuntSYSTEM.hiv","khunt_SECURITY.hiv")
   or FolderPath has @"F:\Oracle\khunt"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName startswith "khunt" or TargetFilePath has "F:\\Oracle\\khunt"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Oracle audit/SQL logs — KHUNT% schema objects and CREATE JAVA SOURCE / dbms_java AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the in-database implant itself, which leaves no file on disk. Per Huntress guidance, search Oracle for object names beginning 'Khunt' and SQL logs for KHUNT%, plus the CREATE JAVA SOURCE / dbms_java / Runtime.exec primitives used to author and publish the six khunt Java objects and khunt_* PL/SQL wrappers. Rationale: This is the article's explicit hunt instruction ('search the Oracle installation for object names beginning Khunt, and SQL logs for KHUNT%'). The Java-execution primitives CREATE JAVA SOURCE + dbms_java + Runtime.exec are the exact mechanism named by both the article and Huntress. No CIM datamodel covers DB audit, so Splunk uses a raw oracle:audit search; Defender/Falcon have no DB-audit telemetry hence empty. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/khunt-malware-sql-injection-oracle • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4206096/attackers-hid-malware-inside-oracle-database-after-sql-injection-breach.html
ATT&CKT1505.001 T1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate developer using CREATE JAVA SOURCE / dbms_java to deploy sanctioned Java stored procedures
  • DBA reviewing or auditing existing Java schema objects
  • A benign schema object legitimately containing the substring 'khunt'
  • Automated ORDS/APEX deployments that emit dbms_java calls
Suppression filter
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("KHUNT","Khunt","runtime.exec") or (SyslogMessage has "CREATE JAVA SOURCE" and SyslogMessage !has "APEX")
Response runbook
1) Triage: in Oracle run SELECT object_name,object_type,owner,created FROM dba_objects WHERE object_name LIKE 'KHUNT%'; confirm any Java source performing Runtime.exec / file I/O. 2) Contain: drop the khunt objects and khunt_* wrappers, revoke CREATE PROCEDURE / JAVA and Runtime.exec file-execution grants from the web-app account, and enforce least privilege. 3) Hunt: correlate the object-creation time with oracle.exe child processes (UC1) and the attacker IP in web logs (UC3); confirm parameterised queries are now enforced on the injectable search endpoint.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("KHUNT","Khunt","CREATE JAVA SOURCE","create java source","dbms_java","DBMS_JAVA","runtime.exec")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, Facility, SeverityLevel, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog (KHUNT OR "CREATE JAVA SOURCE" OR dbms_java OR runtime.exec)
APPLICATION
(index=oracle OR sourcetype IN ("oracle:audit","oracle:audit:xml","oracle:audit:unified")) ("KHUNT" OR "Khunt" OR "CREATE JAVA SOURCE" OR "dbms_java" OR "runtime.exec")
| stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(action) as action values(object_name) as object_name by host, dbuser, os_user, terminal
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;

AWS, Google, and Vercel Agent Flaws Let Attackers Trigger Tools Without Running the Model

The Hacker News
2026-08-06 8 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Security flaws in agent infrastructure from Amazon Web Services (AWS), Google, and Vercel let untrusted or forged instructions reach an agent's tools with no check that a model turn had authorized them. In several of the attack paths, the model never ran at all, so system prompts, content filters, and model-level guardrails never got a chance to intervene. The affected products include Amazon

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer). → [LLM] Exposure inventory: hosts running CoreBreak-vulnerable AWS/Google/Vercel agent framework versions
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Vercel AI SDK harness sandbox-to-host bypass via host-tool-mcp.mjs cmdline spoof · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — AWS, Google, and Vercel Agent Flaws Let Attackers Trigger Tools Without Running
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Vercel AI SDK harness sandbox-to-host bypass via host-tool-mcp.mjs cmdline spoof AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the CoreBreak Vercel path (CVE-2026-64650/64651): untrusted code inside a Linux agent sandbox spawns a process whose command line references the approved helper host-tool-mcp.mjs to satisfy the relay's process-path check and invoke host tools (secret lookups, deploys, cloud API calls) with no model-authorized event. Discriminator is the helper path appearing in a process parented by a package manager, build script, or lifecycle hook rather than the long-lived harness relay. Rationale: Anchors on the exact approved-helper filename host-tool-mcp.mjs (confirmed by cve.threatint.com and the NuclearCoffee mirror) combined with a package-manager/build/lifecycle parent — the article's named untrusted-code vectors — which separates the exploit from the legitimate long-lived harness relay invocation. Cross-checked against: • https://cve.threatint.com/CVE/CVE-2026-64650 • https://cve.threatint.com/CVE/CVE-2026-64651 • https://nuclearcoffee.org/aws-google-and-vercel-agent-flaws-let-attackers-trigger-tools-without-running-the-model/
ATT&CKT1068 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer or CI job legitimately invoking the OpenCode harness helper during interactive debugging where node is the parent
  • A wrapper npm script that intentionally launches the harness (package.json start/dev script) on a build agent
  • Security tooling or SBOM scanners echoing the helper path in a command line during inventory
  • Container image build steps that reference the harness package path while warming caches
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("dev","start") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("code","opencode","codex"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full parent chain (InitiatingProcessCommandLine and its parent) on the host — confirm the helper was spawned from a dependency install/postinstall/build hook rather than an interactive harness session, and check which host-exposed tools (secret reads, deploy, cloud API) fired immediately after. 2) Contain: kill the sandbox session, rotate any secrets/tokens the harness could reach, and pin @ai-sdk/harness-codex>=1.0.29 / @ai-sdk/harness-opencode>=1.0.28 on the affected host/CI runner. 3) Hunt: sweep all build/CI Linux hosts for the same helper-path-in-cmdline pattern and for anomalous cloud API calls (CloudTrail/Azure) originating from those runners' credentials in the minutes after the process fired.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "host-tool-mcp.mjs"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm","npx","node","pnpm","yarn","sh","bash","dash","make","python","python3")
    or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("postinstall","preinstall","prepare","node_modules/.bin","lifecycle")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "host-tool-mcp.mjs"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("npm","npx","node","pnpm","yarn","sh","bash","dash","make","python","python3")
    or ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("postinstall","preinstall","prepare","node_modules/.bin")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Response runbook

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

2026-08-06 15 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a "factory-shipped backdoor" implanted in at least 20 Chinese router models from Zbtlink. According to a new report from VulnCheck, the implant appears in all 21 firmware images currently available from Zbtlink that span more than 2 years. The backdoors are designed such that they start automatically and attempt to beacon to Chinese

ENDLESSDOORS C2 domain resolution (wikaba / epplink / online-string) AICommand & Control High
Hunts DNS lookups for the three hardcoded ENDLESSDOORS phone-home domains embedded in Zbtlink/Wiflyer router firmware. Any internal resolver, router, or host resolving these names indicates an ENDLESSDOORS implant attempting to reach its C2. Rationale: Uses the three exact C2 hostnames named in the article and confirmed in the VulnCheck advisory. wikaba.com is a dynamic-DNS style provider abused for beaconing, so a match is essentially deterministic for a compromised device. Cross-checked against: • https://www.vulncheck.com/advisories/zbt-endlessdoors • https://cyberinsider.com/chinese-zbtlink-wifi-routers-ship-with-endlessdoors-malware/
ATT&CKT1071 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher / IR team detonating the sample in a lab that shares the org resolver
  • Threat-intel sinkhole or passive-DNS collector resolving the IOC for enrichment
  • A vulnerability scanner intentionally probing router firmware behaviour
  • SOAR/EDR automated IOC-validation lookups
  • Analyst manually nslookup-ing the domain during triage
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the ClientIP/resolver source — confirm it is a Zbtlink/Wiflyer router or a host behind one, and check whether the resolution succeeded (Result field) to one of the four C2 IPs. 2) CONTAIN: Sinkhole/block the three domains at the resolver and block egress to 47.107.224.89, 47.100.190.96, 45.32.81.152, 43.248.136.125; isolate the affected router VLAN. 3) HUNT: Pivot on ClientIP for TCP/7000 and TCP/7001 egress and for the kworker/librctl.so file artifacts on any Linux-visible device.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl in~ ("rbdg4nzqadui.wikaba.com", "zbtctl.epplink.net", "online-string.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name in~ ("rbdg4nzqadui.wikaba.com", "zbtctl.epplink.net", "online-string.com")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCode, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ENDLESSDOORS C2 egress to hardcoded IPs on ports 7000/7001 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound TCP to the four hardcoded ENDLESSDOORS C2 IPs, particularly the command channel (TCP/7000) and interactive root-shell callback (TCP/7001). Because the implant dials out, this fires on the beaconing session even though the router has no listening port. Rationale: Four C2 IPs are named verbatim in the article's IOC list and confirmed by VulnCheck; the two service ports (7000 command / 7001 shell) are the fixed rctl protocol ports. Direct IP match to these hosts is deterministic for a compromised device. Cross-checked against: • https://www.vulncheck.com/advisories/zbt-endlessdoors • https://cyberinsider.com/chinese-zbtlink-wifi-routers-ship-with-endlessdoors-malware/
ATT&CKT1571 T1095
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IR/lab detonation of the firmware sample generating real beacons
  • Shared-hosting neighbor: 47.100.x/47.107.x are Alibaba Cloud ranges that may host other legitimate services on different ports
  • Threat-intel scanner or honeypot deliberately connecting to the C2
  • Blue-team purple exercise replaying the IOCs
  • Passive tap capturing decommissioned-but-still-plugged-in router traffic
Suppression filter
| where DestinationPort in (7000, 7001, 53, 443) // 7000/7001 = rctl command+shell; keep 53/443 only if enriching, drop to focus on TP
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm SourceIP is a Zbtlink/Wiflyer router or NATed device; check DestinationPort — 7000/7001 to these IPs is the rctl command/shell channel and is high-severity. 2) CONTAIN: Block egress to all four IPs at the perimeter, deny TCP/7000-7001 outbound from the router VLAN, and physically isolate the appliance. 3) HUNT: Enumerate all Zbtlink/Wiflyer/white-label routers, check for the /usr/sbin/kworker + /usr/lib/librctl.so artifacts, and review DNS logs for the three C2 domains.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("47.107.224.89", "47.100.190.96", "45.32.81.152", "43.248.136.125")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in ("47.107.224.89", "47.100.190.96", "45.32.81.152", "43.248.136.125")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, ApplicationProtocol, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ENDLESSDOORS implant file artifacts on disk (kworker / librctl.so / kworker.cfg / skworker) AIInstallation High
Hunts creation or presence of the four ENDLESSDOORS on-disk artifacts the article lists for filesystem scanning: the fake /usr/sbin/kworker binary, the rctl OpenWrt library /usr/lib/librctl.so, its config /etc/kworker.cfg, and the boot init script /etc/init.d/skworker. Rationale: The four paths are quoted directly from the article's remediation guidance and match the VulnCheck advisory's rctl/OpenWrt package layout (librctl.so, init.d/skworker). A fixed-name file at /usr/sbin/kworker is never legitimate — the real kworker is a kernel thread with no on-disk image. Cross-checked against: • https://www.vulncheck.com/advisories/zbt-endlessdoors • https://securityboulevard.com/2026/08/vulncheck-warns-that-chinese-zbtlink-routers-include-a-backdoor/
ATT&CKT1543 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A malware analyst extracting/copying the artifacts to a forensic workstation for study
  • Backup or imaging tooling re-reading the router filesystem (FileOpenInfo, not write)
  • An unrelated legitimate library also named librctl.so on a non-router Linux host (rare)
  • Config-management repo staging the sample as a known-bad detection test
  • Antivirus quarantine relocating the file, generating a file event
Suppression filter
| where ActionType in~ ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed") // focus on writes, drop read-only FileOpenInfo triage noise
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the host is a Zbtlink/Wiflyer OpenWrt router; capture SHA256 of /usr/sbin/kworker and /usr/lib/librctl.so and confirm none are legitimate OS packages. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the device from the network; do NOT trust an in-place clean — the backdoor is factory-shipped, so plan for firmware replacement/RMA and block the C2 IPs/domains. 3) HUNT: Fleet-wide scan for these four filenames plus /etc/init.d/skworker boot execution and the kworker->/bin/sh reverse-shell chain.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath in~ ("/usr/sbin/kworker", "/usr/lib/librctl.so", "/etc/kworker.cfg", "/etc/init.d/skworker")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath in~ ("/usr/sbin/kworker", "/usr/lib/librctl.so", "/etc/kworker.cfg", "/etc/init.d/skworker")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ENDLESSDOORS kworker userland process masquerading as kernel thread AIInstallation High
Hunts a userland process running from /usr/sbin/kworker. The genuine Linux kworker is a kernel worker thread with no on-disk executable, so a process whose image path is /usr/sbin/kworker is the ENDLESSDOORS implant blending in with real [kworker/*] threads while running as root. Rationale: The article and VulnCheck advisory state the implant 'masquerades as a Linux kernel thread but is actually a userland process running as root' from /usr/sbin/kworker. Because real kworker threads have no executable path, an image path of /usr/sbin/kworker is a deterministic masquerade indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://www.vulncheck.com/advisories/zbt-endlessdoors • https://cyberinsider.com/chinese-zbtlink-wifi-routers-ship-with-endlessdoors-malware/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1036.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate third-party daemon coincidentally installed at /usr/sbin/kworker (extremely rare and itself suspicious)
  • Malware-analysis sandbox running the extracted sample
  • EDR sensor mislabeling a bracketed kernel [kworker/*] thread — filter empty command lines
  • Detection-engineering test harness deploying a benign binary named kworker
  • Container image built with a decoy kworker for red-team purposes
Suppression filter
| where isnotempty(ProcessCommandLine) and FolderPath =~ "/usr/sbin/kworker" // exclude bracketed kernel [kworker/*] threads which have no path/cmdline
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the process image path is /usr/sbin/kworker (not the bracketed kernel thread) and that it runs as uid=0; note child processes and network sockets to TCP/7000-7001. 2) CONTAIN: Kill the process, isolate the router, and block the four C2 IPs/three domains — but treat the device as firmware-compromised (persistence survives reboot via /etc/init.d/skworker). 3) HUNT: Look for the /bin/sh reverse-shell child of this process and enumerate all Zbtlink/Wiflyer models for the same masquerade.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath =~ "/usr/sbin/kworker" or ProcessCommandLine has "/usr/sbin/kworker"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "kworker" and isnotempty(ActingProcessCommandLine)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "/usr/sbin/kworker"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
